summary: Defines the procedure to register RTP payload formats as MIME subtypes for audio, video, and other media, so text-based protocols can name what is in an RTP stream. It also registers the payload formats from the RTP audio/video profile. It is a proposed standard and was replaced by RFCs 4855 and 4856.

eli5.summary: Every kind of media stream needs a name tag. This memo sets up how to give names to the formats used in live streaming.

questions: mime types for rtp payload formats
what is an rtp payload format
how does a mime type map to sdp
subtitle: How to give each RTP payload format a MIME name, and the first batch of names for audio and video.

tldr.problem: Text-based protocols and formats need a standard way to say what kind of media an RTP stream carries.
tldr.mechanism: RTP payload formats are registered as MIME subtypes under audio, video or other types, with a fixed set of parameters that map onto SDP lines. The memo also registers every payload format from the RTP audio/video profile.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3555 has been obsoleted by RFC 4855 and RFC 4856, so those are the current references.

today: RFC 3555 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4855 and RFC 4856. It was also updated by RFC 3625 and RFC 4629.

sections.title: Why RTP Formats Need MIME Names
sections.content:
The MIME registration procedure was designed for multimedia sent by email, but the MIME namespace now names media for other transports too. RFC 3555 defines how to register a MIME subtype name for a payload format of the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP), so that a text-based format or control protocol can say what an RTP transmission contains.

The memo also registers every payload format defined in the RTP Profile for Audio and Video Conferences (RFC 3551) as a subtype of audio or video. Some of these may also be used for transfer modes other than RTP.
sections.eli5: A label on a lunchbox tells you what is inside before you open it. MIME names are labels for streams of sound and video.

sections.title: The Registration Procedure
sections.content:
Registering an RTP payload type follows the normal MIME procedure and template from RFC 2048, plus some extra items. The published specification must describe the encoding and the payload format, usually by pointing to an RTP payload format RFC, and it MUST include the RTP timestamp clock rate. If the format has no fixed clock rate, a rate parameter is required.

Most audio formats can take an optional channels parameter. Any format can take ptime, the recommended milliseconds of media per packet, and maxptime, the most media allowed in one packet. The encoding considerations MUST say that the type can be sent over RTP.

Three cases are covered. A type that is not yet registered gets a new registration. A type that exists for non-RTP use gets updated to say it may also travel over RTP, with RTP-only parameters clearly marked. A type that exists for RTP can likewise be updated for non-RTP use.
sections.eli5: To get a name, you fill in a form: what the format is, how fast it ticks, and how much sound goes in each packet. If the name already exists, you just add a note.

sections.title: Mapping to SDP
sections.content:
A media type is written as type "/" subtype *(";" parameter). The Session Description Protocol (SDP), commonly used to describe RTP sessions, has a fixed mapping from those pieces.

  • The MIME type (for example audio) goes in the SDP m= line as the media name.
  • The subtype goes in a=rtpmap as the encoding name, along with rate as the clock rate and channels as the encoding parameters.
  • ptime and maxptime go in the a=ptime and a=maxptime attributes.
  • Any format-specific parameters go in a=fmtp.

The set of format-specific parameters is defined by the RFC that specifies the payload format. A MIME registration MUST NOT extend it without a matching revision of that specification. Names and parameter names are case-insensitive.
sections.eli5: The MIME name is the short version, and SDP is the long form on a form. This section says which box each part of the name goes into.

sections.title: The Audio and Video Registrations
sections.content:
Section 4 is the bulk of the document. Each of the 22 audio subtypes (from audio/DVI4 to audio/VDVI) and 13 video subtypes (from video/BT656 to video/nv) gets its own template. Most name RFC 3551 as the published specification and say the type is only defined for transfer via RTP.

A few have extras. audio/G723 has optional bitrate (5.3 or 6.3) and annexa parameters. audio/G729 and its variants have an annexb parameter. audio/L16 was already registered by RFC 2586 for non-RTP transports, so that registration is folded in and extended; it adds emphasis and channel-order options.

audio/RED has a required pt parameter listing the payload types it carries. Its published specification is RFC 2198, and the memo shows how the list maps into a=fmtp by dropping the name and changing commas to slashes.
sections.eli5: This is the big list of name tags: one for each sound and picture style. Most are plain, and a few have extra settings.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The registration procedure does not impose security considerations of its own, and the registrations themselves do not impose risks, though some state considerations specific to them. The memo notes that several audio and video encodings are well suited to hiding data using steganography.

For the security of RTP transport itself, including encryption when confidentiality is needed, it points to RFC 3550.
sections.eli5: Giving a stream a name tag is safe. But a secret message can be hidden inside a song or a picture, and encryption is how you keep a stream private.

data.title: audio/L16 in SDP
data.code:
audio/L16; rate=48000; channels=2; ptime=5; emphasis=50-15

m=audio 49170 RTP/AVP 97
a=rtpmap:97 L16/48000/2
a=fmtp:97 emphasis=50-15
a=ptime:5
